Pele Yoetz 22:2: And for every food of which one eats an olive's volume, and every drink of which one drinks a quarter-log, one must recite the concluding blessing, each according to its own blessing. And the trouble is that many of the common people do not know the formula of "Me'ein Shalosh" [the abbreviated Grace], which must be recited after pastry, after wine, and after fruits of the seven species, such as fresh and dried grapes, raisins, figs, pomegranates, and olives - and especially when one must mention the specific occasion - and therefore they either recite "who creates many souls," which is a blessing in vain, or they recite no blessing at all. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Berachot 35a): whoever enjoys this world without a blessing has committed a trespass. What is the remedy? Let him go to a sage and let him teach him. And this is a great principle: whoever wishes to serve God as befits us, being Jews, believers, sons of believers, in the Torah and in all the words of the Sages and in reward and punishment, should not be ashamed or embarrassed to go to a sage and let him teach him, and let the formula of the blessings and other necessary matters be written for him in clear script, and let him guide him in the way of truth and lead him in the way of the good. And truly they said (Proverbs 13:20): "he who walks with the wise shall become wise."
Pele Yoetz 22:3: And a man should tremble before putting anything into his mouth without a blessing - for if one who robs a king is liable to death by the king's law, all the more so one who robs the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, and the congregation of Israel. And also one who misappropriates sacred property is liable to death, and they have said that one who enjoys [this world] without a blessing is as though he misappropriated sacred property and as though he robbed the Holy One, blessed be He, and the congregation of Israel (Berachot 35b). And they further said that food and drink are the nourishment of the body, while the blessings are the nourishment of the soul, causing an abundance of holiness to rest upon the eating and the drinking. And this is the meaning of the verse (Deuteronomy 8:3): "for man does not live by bread alone, but by everything that proceeds from the mouth of the LORD does man live." And this is also [the meaning of] "the righteous eats to satisfy his soul" (Proverbs 13:25). And truly, these who eat and drink without a blessing - were it not that we judge them favorably, that habit has become for them a nature, to the point that they do not remember that a blessing is required - would deserve great punishment, for what trouble and what expense is it to say a brief blessing and bless for the good that the LORD our God gives us - a thing customary even among ordinary people, that one fill his mouth with praise and give thanks for every kind of good he receives from another. And in addition, our merciful God counts it as a mitzvah for us that we bless Him, and establishes for us reward for the blessing - a good and a blessing. Is there a sweeter palate than this? Certainly, whoever does not wish to bless has nothing but evil of heart. And it is fitting for a person to be very careful and stand guard not to forget to bless, until he becomes so accustomed that his mouth shall not open, nor shall it accept that anything be put into it without a blessing - for just as they said (Sotah 38b): whoever blesses is blessed, so correspondingly, whoever does not bless brings a curse upon himself.
Pele Yoetz 22:4: And this evil of eating and drinking without a blessing is more common among women, who are not expert in the matters of blessings and eat and drink without a blessing, like the Hebrew women in Egypt. And this mitzvah falls upon the fathers of daughters, and the husband is obligated regarding his wife to teach her, for they have said (Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 169:2) that it is forbidden to feed one whom he knows does not bless, and the man is punished for the members of his household - therefore he is obligated to teach her or hire a teacher for her. And this is a great principle: that a person should not worry about the expense, nor consider it a waste of time to occupy himself with these matters, teaching the people and the members of his household knowledge and bringing them merit and the like - for what use is time and money to us if not to do therewith the will and give peace of mind to our Former? And sometimes the nullification of Torah is its very fulfillment, in the manner of what is written (Psalms 119:126), "it is time to act for the LORD, they have nullified Your Torah." Happy is he whose ways are such, to do a thing in its proper time as it should be done. And it is fitting to strive with all one's strength to search the books or hear from the mouths of scholars, and write down the text of the blessings and the laws of the blessings which he is not expert in, until he becomes accustomed and they are fluent in his mouth. And likewise it is fitting to strive to be well-versed among people, to be expert in the blessing for bridegrooms and the blessing for the host and the like. And how very much one must be careful with the blessing of the new moon, which is [likened to] receiving the presence of the Shechinah. And truly they said (Berachot 50a, Yerushalmi ibid. 21:8): from a person's blessings one can tell whether he is learned or ignorant. And how good it is for a man to strive to know the meaning of the words in the blessings he recites, and to take care to have proper intention in the blessings he recites - for they have said (Midrash Shmuel, Avot 2:15, and see the introduction to the Ya'avetz prayer book): prayer or a blessing without intention is like a body without a soul.
Pele Yoetz 22:5: And the essential service of God, blessed be His Name, is service of the heart (Sanhedrin 106b, see Rashi there; Ta'anit 2a). Therefore one must strive very much to intend the meaning of the words in everything that comes from his mouth - prayers, blessings, and studies. And one mitzvah draws another - that he be aroused through these matters to serve his Creator a complete service, a perfect service, with fear and love and great joy, and thereby he shall not come to serve God in a casual manner, as many ignorant people do, who, while blessing or praying or studying, raise their voice with force to rebuke someone or to hint at something they want, and say "shh, shh, shh," and joke around. And if they pictured to themselves that they were speaking in a foreign tongue and speaking before the king while making these rebukes and hints, shame and disgrace and wrath would cover them. Therefore this too deserves attention - to go to a sage who shall teach him the prayers and blessings in the vernacular, and let him not be ashamed nor wither, so that he can serve his Creator a complete service, for this applies to every person. And even one who knows the blessings and their laws sometimes has doubts about various matters of blessings - for all of this, care and diligence are needed, to withdraw his hand or act in a beneficial manner so as not to enter into a doubt of enjoying [something] without a blessing, God forbid. And every God-fearing person should discharge the requirements of all halachic authorities in matters that depend on a dispute. "And clean hands add strength" (Job 17:9) not to come to the common forgetfulness, and he shall set up markers for himself to remember and to bless, especially with the concluding blessing for water drunk before extending credit [i.e. before a meal, an idiom], and the blessing "Asher Yatzar" and the like. And of this and similar matters we say: happy is the man who listens to Your commandments, and places Your Torah and Your word upon his heart.
Pele Yoetz 22:6: And there are many of the common people who think they are reciting a blessing, but their blessing is invalid because they skip several words and letters, and they do two evils - they enjoy [something] without a blessing and they mention the Name in vain. And this is the fruit of haste, which is a sick evil, for even though he recites the entire blessing, doing so hastily to bless the King of glory with a rushed blessing is worthy of disgrace and wrath - this is not one who blesses, but one who blasphemes (Sanhedrin 6b). Happy is the man who fears the LORD - let him accept upon himself with all his strength and strive with great might to recite all his blessings aloud, letter by letter, word by word, with a willing spirit and a joyful heart - and this applies to every person, that he should strive with all his strength to fulfill every good thing as is fitting, and this is the sign of whether he is a good man.
Pele Yoetz 22:7: And regarding blessings whose obligation a person discharges by hearing them, such as Kiddush, Havdalah, the "Me'ein Shalosh" blessing, and the blessing of Hallel, one must be extra careful that his ears be attentive to the blessing and not lose even a single word - and needless to say that he should not speak in between, for then he does not discharge his obligation at all, and it is found that he remains without Kiddush and without Havdalah, or enjoys [something] without a blessing. And likewise, during the repetition of the Amidah one must stand guard to hear each blessing properly and answer Amen properly. And here too the affliction has spread, that many of the common people speak to one another during the repetition of the Amidah, and they do several evil things: first, they speak in the synagogue, which is a great prohibition, as written in its place. Second, they speak during the repetition of the Amidah, which our master wrote in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim 124:7) is a transgression in his hands and he is rebuked for it - but now many have trampled upon it, and it has become like something permitted, with no one to protest against them. Third, they lose much good in [failing to fulfill] "hearing is like answering, and answering is like blessing." And it is known that our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Chullin 87a) that the reward of a blessing is ten gold coins. And how much a person labors to earn ten gold coins, yet these fools throw away several gold coins with their own hands without paying attention to overcome their inclination even slightly. And this is a great principle in the Torah: that one should reckon the reward of a mitzvah against the loss of a transgression. And let him strengthen himself to overcome his inclination, and the LORD shall be his help. And it is the custom of men of deeds to hold the prayer book in their hands during the repetition, as if listening silently to the prayer.
Pele Yoetz 22:8: It is written (Proverbs 22:9): "one who is good of eye shall be blessed [yevorach]." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sotah 38b): do not read it "yevorach" [shall be blessed] but "yavrich" [shall cause blessing] - for whoever is good to the world shall bless [others], and one who blesses Israel is himself also blessed, as it is written (Genesis 12:3), "and I shall bless those who bless you." Correspondingly, one who curses Israel injures his own soul, as it is written (ibid.), "and one who curses you I shall curse." And since it is written (Proverbs 3:27), "do not withhold good from its owners when it is in your power to do it," it is fitting to always strive to bless Israel - perhaps it shall be at a time of favor and his words shall bear fruit. And therefore even one who is blessed should himself bless in return and say, "and the same to you, sir." As known from the incident brought in the Talmud (Megillah 27b), that Rav gave a blessing to Rav Huna, and I responded [with it], and Rav was exacting with me for not having said to him, "and the same to you, sir." And it is found that if his blessing bears fruit, he thereby performs an act of kindness for his fellow, and in any case gives peace of mind to his Maker, for it is good in the eyes of the LORD to bless Israel, and it shall be counted a mitzvah for him - for this is the reasoning of some halachic authorities who permit one to bless his fellow before he recites the blessing over something sweet, and this is not a case of prioritizing human honor over the honor of Heaven, for this too is the honor of Heaven. And especially since, if he tastes the sweet thing first, sometimes he shall speak before swallowing it and commit a transgression - therefore it is better to bless one's fellow before reciting the blessing.
Pele Yoetz 22:9: And it is fitting for a person to strive always that people bless him, and to flee greatly from quarreling with anyone and bringing a curse upon himself - for our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 7a, Megillah 15a): let not the blessing of an ordinary person be light in your eyes, and let not the curse of an ordinary person be light in your eyes - and they bring there instances of gentiles who blessed or cursed the great men of the generation, and it was fulfilled in them, for everything depends on the time and the moment - there is a time of favor and there is a moment of His anger. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Ruth Rabbah 7:15): were it not for the blessing of the old women to Naomi, the "eggs" [i.e., the offspring] of the House of David would have been uprooted. Therefore let every person desire a blessing, and especially crave the blessing of Torah scholars and the righteous, and pursue it, for their blessing is close to being fulfilled. And in any case he shall carry a blessing from the LORD for valuing Torah and the righteousness of the LORD, and this is included among those who honor the Torah and those who study it. And also let the Torah scholar himself be good of eye and shall be blessed, and whoever desires his blessing, let him bless him with many blessings, for what does it cost him to cause good and let his fellow benefit while he himself loses nothing - and it shall be counted to him as a mitzvah.
Pele Yoetz 22:10: And they said in the Zohar (part 1, page 227) that when a person wishes to bless his fellow or his son and the like, he must first bless the Holy One, blessed be He, and if he does not first bless the Holy One, blessed be He, those blessings shall not be fulfilled. And such was the custom of the master, our teacher Rabbi Yosef Chazak, of blessed memory, that when a person came to him to be blessed, he would place his hand on his head and say, "blessed be the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He," and afterward bless that man or that youth and the like. So wrote our teacher Rabbi Yosef Ades [or similar], of blessed memory, in the book "Devash LePi" - see there. [And so I too am accustomed, when blessing my son or anyone who requests my blessing, to place my hand on his head and say: blessed be the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and may He in His mercy guard you from all evil, may He guard your soul and guide you with good counsel from before Him, and may you be complete in attributes and in opinions and in every kind of perfection, and may no mishap come from your own hand, nor anything improper, and may no guilt roll about through you, and may you find favor and good sense in the eyes of God and man, and may nothing distract you from the service of God, blessed be His Name. May the LORD bless you and keep you. May the LORD make His face shine upon you and be gracious to you. May the LORD lift up His face to you and grant you peace (Numbers 6:24, 26). May your father and mother rejoice, and may she who bore you exult (Proverbs 23:25). May God make you like Ephraim and like Manasseh (Genesis 48:20). And for my daughters or my female relatives I bless thus: blessed be the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and may He in His mercy guard you from all evil, may He guard your soul and guide you with good counsel from before Him, and may you be a woman of valor who fears the LORD (and if she is unmarried: and may you be given into the bosom of a God-fearing man in the lifetime of your father and mother), and may you not be among the bereaved or the barren or the widowed, but rather may your children be a joy to you for length of days and years of life, and may you be complete in attributes and in opinions and in every kind of perfection, and may you find favor and good sense in the eyes of God and in the eyes of your husband, and may you rejoice in the offspring of your own body. May the LORD bless you and keep you, and so on.] And at the moment he blesses, his heart shall tremble within him over the fact that people do not recognize his own faults and yet esteem him and his blessing, and let him say in his heart: I know of myself that I am not worthy and it is not fitting that my blessing bear fruit, but I bless nonetheless, perhaps I shall find a time of favor and my blessing shall be accepted from the LORD, who hears the prayer of every mouth.
Pele Yoetz 22:11: And when one gives a greeting of peace to his fellow, he shall intend to say: peace be to you. And the one who answers says: peace, blessing, and good be to you. And likewise when one says "Shabbat Shalom," he shall intend to say: by the merit of the Sabbath, may peace be to you - and the one who answers says: by the merit of the Sabbath may you have peace and may you be blessing others. And likewise a person must strive to receive the blessing of the poor and the destitute, for "the LORD hears the destitute" (Psalms 69:34). And guard yourself and guard your soul very much not to bring a curse upon yourself from Torah scholars or from the poor and destitute, for their bite is the bite of a fox and their sting is the sting of a scorpion, and the LORD shall plead their cause and take the life of those who rob them (Proverbs 22:23). And Torah scholars and the poor and every person must guard their mouths very much not to curse anyone and not to cause anyone to be punished on their account, for whoever causes his fellow to be punished is not admitted into the presence of the Holy One, blessed be He (Shabbat 149b), as written on this in its place.
Pele Yoetz 22:12: And all the more so a person must exert himself and strive very much to receive the blessing of his father and mother - and even if he does not dine at their table and his dwelling is far from them, he should not be lax about going every Sabbath eve and its day and on the festivals to kiss their hands and receive their blessing - for besides the fact that the blessing is close to being fulfilled since they bless him from the heart and from the soul, wholeheartedly, like a father's compassion for his children, moreover it shall be counted a mitzvah for him for honoring his father and mother, and he shall receive his reward. And they said in the Midrash (Bereishit Rabbah 63) that all the good and the kingdom possessed by the seed of Esau came about because he valued his father's blessing and cried out a great and bitter cry (Genesis 27:34), saying, "bless me too, my father." And let him guard his soul very much not to bring a curse upon himself from his father and mother - for even though they do not curse him from the heart and do not wish to see evil befall even his smallest fingernail, and immediately regret it, nevertheless, combined with the sin he committed in causing his father or mother distress and anger, there is reason to fear that evil may come upon him, God forbid. Therefore let father and mother have mercy on their children and not curse them, as shall be written below under the entry "Kelalah" [curse], with the help of Heaven. And one who blesses shall carry a blessing from the LORD, and just as a blessing is good in its proper time, so there is a time when its absence is better than its presence.
Pele Yoetz 22:13: Regarding blessing the LORD, one must be very careful not to recite an unnecessary blessing or a blessing in vain, which transgresses "you shall not take [the Name of the LORD in vain]" - and this is found among the common people who wish to be pious and bless over every single thing, and sometimes they stumble and fall into the prohibition of a vain blessing or an unnecessary blessing - but "he who walks with the wise shall become wise" (Proverbs 13:20). And likewise regarding blessing one's fellow it is written (ibid. 27:14): "one who blesses his fellow with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted a curse to him." And there are two explanations for this: first, that there is a prohibition against greeting one's fellow with peace or blessing him before prayer, for it is considered as though he made [that person] into a high place [of idolatrous worship, i.e. prioritized him over God]. And the second way: if he blesses his fellow in front of others, he causes him harm, in that others shall pounce upon him, thinking it fitting that he do good to them even more than he did to this one - while he did not intend this and did not think so in his heart, for reasons known to himself - and it is found that he caused divisions and grievances to increase against him. Therefore every clever person shall act with knowledge, and in every place where there is reason to fear that harm might befall his fellow in any way if the matter becomes known, a faithful spirit conceals the matter.
Pele Yoetz 23:1: The Synagogue - The mitzvah of rising early for the synagogue is among the matters whose fruits a person enjoys in this world while the principal remains for him in the World to Come. And it is known that they said in the Talmud (Berachot 8a) that this is what benefited the people of Babylon in reaching old age, as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said to his sons: rise early and stay late at the synagogue, so that you may prolong your lives. And one who arrives early among the first ten receives reward equal to all who come after him, and especially one who arrives first of all - the Holy Zohar (Terumah, page 131) went to great lengths in his praise, that he stands at the level of a righteous man and it is a great repair for the blemish of the covenant, and he becomes a beloved friend of the Holy One, blessed be He. Whoever hears such things and does not strive with all his strength to be first, or at least among the first ten, to give peace of mind to his Maker, who pays a good reward to those who do His will...
Pele Yoetz 23:2: And there are many who come early to the synagogue and could be among the first ten, but choose instead to sit outside in the synagogue courtyard to increase conversation, thereby giving up their own merit to others - they do not take it to heart and are not particular that another precede them, because they do not know what this mitzvah is.
Pele Yoetz 23:3: And there are those who make of the synagogue courtyard a gathering place of the common people, sitting there on Sabbaths and festivals until the cantor reaches "Baruch She'amar," and only then enter the synagogue and pray in a skipped or abbreviated manner, or alone. Woe to them, for they have done evil to their own souls, and it is evil and bitter that they have forsaken the LORD. And whoever has the power to protest should protest against them. And whoever fears the word of the LORD should not sit with them. And it is known what they said about the master Ari, that he was never among the first ten, because there were people who would arrive even before dawn, whereas he wished to go to the synagogue wrapped in his tallit and crowned with tefillin - for the Holy Zohar went to great lengths in praising one who goes from his house to the synagogue wrapped in his tallit and crowned with tefillin, for the heavenly hosts proclaim before him: give honor to the image of the King! Correspondingly, one who enters the synagogue without tefillin and says "I shall bow toward Your holy sanctuary in awe of You," the Holy One, blessed be He, says: where is My fear? Behold, he testifies a false testimony. See the Holy Zohar, Parashat Va'etchanan (page 265).
Pele Yoetz 23:4: Behold, therefore, happy is the man who does this - to leave his house wrapped in his tallit and crowned with tefillin - and let him not worry about being among the first ten, for it is a mitzvah to delay so as not to hasten to put them on while it is still night, and especially on winter nights, when the moon is shining and the day is cloudy, extra caution is needed. In any case, he should not fail to put them on in the synagogue courtyard if his house is far from the synagogue and there is reason to fear the appearance of arrogance or the mockery of the complacent - but he should not enter the synagogue without tefillin.
Pele Yoetz 23:5: And before entering the synagogue, one must ask permission by reciting the verse "and I, through the abundance of Your kindness" - not as many do, who do not know [better] and say it after entering, but rather he should linger at the entrance like one who trembles to enter the house of a high and exalted king, awesome and fearsome, and ask permission by reciting the verse "and I, through the abundance of Your kindness." And before this verse, he must first recite the morning blessings, for if he has not yet recited the blessings over the Torah, some say he may not recite it. And he must vary [the wording slightly] and say: "and I, through the abundance of His kindness, I shall come to His house; I shall bow toward His holy sanctuary in awe of Him." And how good and how pleasant it would be to establish a box for the poor of the city and place it at the entrance to the synagogue, and bore a hole in its lid, so that everyone who enters the synagogue first give a coin there to charity - the wealthy shall give more and the poor shall give no less than a coin each time - and say, "as for me, I shall behold Your face in righteousness" (Psalms 17:15). This is a great and very beneficial thing. (And I am accustomed to reciting this order, and sometimes I add words as the need of the hour requires, for every trouble that should not come - let the wise man hear and increase learning [Proverbs 1:5].)
Pele Yoetz 23:6: And it is good to say: behold, I am going to the synagogue to unify the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah (in the morning) with the right arm (and in the evening) with the left arm, and I am prepared to give charity to give peace of mind to our Former, for the elevation of the Shechinah of our strength, and for the atonement of my sins and my forefathers' sins, and for the elevation of their souls, and for the elevation of the soul of Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes, so that the merit of Rabbi Meir Ba'al HaNes shield us that we may serve our Creator a complete service, a perfect service, for length of days and years of life, and no evil may befall us and no affliction come near our dwelling, and so that by the merit of Rabbi Meir all our offspring be a holy seed, a seed of worthy men, complete in attributes and in opinions in every kind of perfection. God of Rabbi Meir, answer me. "As for me, I shall behold Your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with Your likeness" (Psalms, ibid.). "In the house of God we walked with the throng" (ibid. 55:15). "How awesome is this place - this is nothing other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven" (Genesis 28:17). And "I, through the abundance," and so on. However, he can only say all this when he comes early, when no one else is in the synagogue - but when there are people inside and out, it looks like arrogance to stand and linger at the entrance of the synagogue; but he can say it beforehand at home or on his way if the street is clean, and in any case he should not fail to say, at the entrance of the synagogue, at least the verse "and I, through the abundance," and so on.
Pele Yoetz 23:7: And afterward, the heart's intentions are the essentials - one must be fearful, trembling, and shuddering at how he shall enter the King's palace, a vessel full of shame and disgrace. And he shall intend, when saying "and I, through the abundance of Your kindness, shall come to Your house," that he is not worthy to enter the King's palace except for the greatness of His kindness and by the merit of the early patriarchs. And he shall intend: "Your kindness" alludes to Abraham our father, peace be upon him, the man of kindness; "Your sanctuary" alludes to Isaac, who was sanctified upon the altar; "in awe of You" alludes to Jacob, who said, "how awesome is this place." And by their merit we are supported in entering the holy place.
Pele Yoetz 23:8: And from this the living person shall take to heart to stand there in dread, in fear, trembling and shuddering, and not to engage there in idle conversation, God forbid, out of fear of the Shechinah that dwells there. And it is known that the Holy Zohar (Terumah, page 131) went to great lengths in severity regarding one who speaks in the synagogue, saying that he treats the Shechinah with disgrace and has no share in the God of Israel - see there. A man's hair should stand on end at seeing its severity, and hearts ache that this has become like something permitted to many of the common people, and it is no help that they sometimes hear its severity from those who preach among the people, and nevertheless do not abandon their evil custom, and "the world follows its custom." Woe to these creatures on the day of judgment and the day of rebuke. And this affliction has spread especially in days of celebration and rejoicing, festivals, the nights of Simchat Beit HaSho'evah, Simchat Torah, the days of Purim, and the like - because of the sweetness of the joy, they increase in laughter and levity. And whoever has the power to protest should protest for the sake of His honored Name, and whoever does not have the power to protest should guard his own soul to be like one mute, not opening his mouth.
Pele Yoetz 23:9: And there is one who wants to be careful not to speak in the synagogue, but when others speak to him it seems to him a matter of shame and arrogance not to answer them and say that he does not speak in the synagogue, and so he too speaks with a pained heart until in the end it becomes like something permitted to him. But the man who fears the LORD shall let a trembling seize him over the severity of the matter, and shall not be ashamed before anyone, and shall say with a full mouth: I do not speak in the synagogue - for this is like one from whom others wish to take a vast fortune or to kill him, who does not worry about shame or anything else, but hastens to find himself an escape. All the more so must one have mercy on his own soul and on the honor of his Maker. This is a great principle: not to commit any transgression and not to refrain from fulfilling any mitzvah out of shame, and of this they said (Avot 5:20): be bold as a leopard to do the will of your Father in Heaven. And one who is careful of this, besides being saved from a severe punishment, is also given reward as one who performs a mitzvah, for he fulfills the mitzvah "and you shall revere My sanctuary" (Leviticus 19:30) - for the synagogue is a small sanctuary and one must revere it.
Pele Yoetz 23:10: And included in the reverence for the synagogue is that he should not raise his voice there with force, even to call someone or to protest against others doing something improper, but rather, when he needs to speak, let him go to them and speak to them quietly, with pleasant speech and with gravity, as one standing in the King's palace. And the eye sees how people stand before the officers of the land and its judges with great honor, with no sound and no voice heard, a thin, still voice - over this let all who grieve, grieve, for even the idolaters, who glorify themselves through their idols, when sitting in their houses of worship stand with great honor, in dread and fear. And it is true that one who stands before a judge has his eyes upon what is before him, and if he wishes to speak some superfluous word, the judge's own anger and the wrath of the king of the angels of death shall frighten him - but not so one who stands in the synagogue, who does not see what is before him, and one is not punished immediately and at once, but is allowed to go on his way as he wishes, while the inclination nearby stands at his right hand to incite him, seducing him doubly to transgress against his Maker's will - this is the whole evil of man upon the earth. But the obligation of a person who is a Jew and believes with complete faith in the existence of the LORD, an awesome and fearsome King everywhere - the whole earth is full of His glory, and especially His light and the resting of His Shechinah are revealed in His holy sanctuary - and He watches over all the ways of the sons of man to give each man according to his ways, and repays even for light conversation, whether for good or for less good - today to do them and tomorrow to receive reward and punishment, and it is in a person's power to overcome his inclination, and such is his obligation and such is fitting for him, and this applies to every person. Happy is the man who fears the LORD everywhere, and all the more so in His holy sanctuary - let there be silence before Him, and let his voice not be heard when he enters the holy place to speak with his fellow. And the early sages set a great fence: not to speak with one's fellow even words of Torah, so that a listener not suspect them and so that they not teach a leniency for themselves.
Pele Yoetz 23:11: And the caution not to speak in the synagogue applies even when it is not the time of prayer - but during the time of prayer, one must be careful not to speak even outside the synagogue, from the beginning of the prayer to its end. And it is known, the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Berachot 6a), that a person's prayer is heard only in the synagogue. And they further said (ibid. 8a): whoever has a synagogue in his city and does not enter it is called a bad neighbor and brings exile upon himself. Therefore it is fitting to strive very much to pray in the synagogue - even if he must pray alone, let him go to the synagogue and pray - and all the more so must he strive greatly to pray in the synagogue with the congregation, and not pray alone, nor at home even with a quorum, unless under great duress, for he loses much good. And this suffices for one who has a good heart, for one who does not have a good heart, such words as these shall not enter him.
Pele Yoetz 24:1: The Study House - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sukkah 52b, Kiddushin 30a): if this scoundrel [the evil inclination] confronts you, drag him to the study house. If he is like stone, he shall melt; if he is like iron, he shall shatter. And the study house is the place where Torah is studied publicly. And it is fitting to designate a place in every city that shall be set aside as a study house, to teach Torah publicly. If there are Torah scholars in the city, let them all gather together daily or nightly, and let them have a fixed session to study with depth and dialectic wherever their hearts desire - Scripture, Mishnah, Talmud, or the halachic authorities and the like. For our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 8a): the LORD loves the gates distinguished by halachah more than all the synagogues and study houses, and the Holy One, blessed be He, has in His world only the four cubits of halachah alone. And for the rest of the common people, let there be a fixed place for them to study publicly the daily order of Chok LeYisrael, and in the evening let them also study publicly Scripture and Mishnah, and let them engage some Torah scholar to expound to them words of Aggadah and teach them laws - and through this they shall fulfill "and you shall meditate in it day and night" (Joshua 1:8). And likewise every Friday night let them establish a study session and study to know the statutes of God and His teachings, and other studies such as Mishnayot, Idra, and Psalms. And how good and how pleasant it would be to study once a week the order of the 613 mitzvot, to fulfill "so we render the words of our lips as calves" (Hosea 14:3).
Pele Yoetz 24:2: And it is good for a man not to withhold much good from himself, and not to keep himself away from the study house even once. And let not his inclination mislead him with vain and misleading claims, for great is the power of Torah studied by the many, for favor and peace of mind before our Father in Heaven, and all the more so in the study of dialectic and debate - for Torah is acquired only in company (Berachot 63b). And it is written (Jeremiah 50:36), "a sword against the linguists [badim]" - and our Sages, of blessed memory, explained (Berachot, ibid.; Ta'anit 7a) this as: a sword against the enemies of Torah scholars who sit alone [bad bevad] and occupy themselves with Torah [alone] - and not only that, but they become foolish, and not only that, but they come to sin. And it is written (Proverbs 27:17), "iron sharpens iron," and so on. And it was taught (Avot 6:5): Torah is acquired through the dialectic discussion of colleagues. And especially to clarify the law thoroughly, company is greatly needed - for they said (Sanhedrin 7b, see there) that when Rava was about to rule on a case of a possibly non-kosher animal, he would gather together all the butchers of Mechoza, saying: so that if there was some flaw [in my reasoning], correction should come from many [advisors]. And we, orphans of orphans, what shall we answer after this? However, the study must be conducted according to law and precept - that they be pleasant to one another in halachah, and not wound one another in halachah, and one should not say "accept my view," nor entrench himself stubbornly on a point of halachah, but rather each shall state his opinion once - if they accept it, they accept it, and if not, what does it matter to him - and he should not exert great effort to refute his fellow's words. And let a person be God-fearing, acknowledging the truth and accepting the truth from whoever states it, without shame, for "the acknowledgment of the Rabbis is itself their praise." And if the obligation of love between one man and his fellow is great for every person, all the more so between colleagues who study together - for the master Ari wrote that there must be intense love between them, love of the soul, like one body, like one man.
Pele Yoetz 24:3: And all who go to study houses should be careful to sit there in dread and fear, all sitting together bound as one, studying in clear speech and with holy pleasantness. And when the sage expounds, all shall stand in silence, their ears attentive to the words of the preacher with affection, to keep and to do and to fulfill - and in any case they shall not, God forbid, engage in laughter or levity or idle talk like those who sit in the corners in the study house, for the sanctity of the study house is greater than the sanctity of the synagogue (Megillah 27a), and the Shechinah precedes [to be present at] every gathering of ten (Sanhedrin 39a). And one must sit there in dread and fear - whoever does this shall have his portion among those who sit in the study house, and if not, absence is better than the presence of evil - for if one goes there to sleep and to smoke all night and to engage in idle talk and laughter and levity, the LORD shall say (Isaiah 1:12): who asked this of you, to trample My courts and come to My house to be a sinner and cause others to sin - would it not be better for you to rest on your bed at home? But if he can overcome his inclination to sit there properly, occupied with Torah or listening to teachings, let him not fail to go to the study house even once - for our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Chagigah 9b): what is a deficiency that cannot be counted? This: one whose colleagues were counted for a mitzvah matter and he was not counted with them. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Devarim Rabbah 7:1) that for every day a person keeps himself from going to the assembly below, he is pushed away in the future from the assembly above, and he loses much good of public study, and loses the knowledge of the statutes of God and His teachings, and loses much good from the Kaddishes [recited there], and many such good things. Therefore, whoever loves his own soul shall always have his portion among those who sit in the study house. Happy is he whose labor is in Torah and who gives peace of mind to his Maker.
Pele Yoetz 25:1: Disgrace - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Avot 4:3): do not despise any person, for there is no person who does not have his hour. They meant that even a lowly convert should not be disgraced or cursed, for their kingdoms follow after their patrons [in the heavenly spheres] (Pesachim 113a). And all the more so regarding a Jew - one should not disgrace any Jew, for God made man in the image of God, and one who disgraces a Jew is as though he disgraces the Shechinah, God forbid - as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 58b): one who slaps his fellow's cheek is as though he slaps the cheek of the Shechinah. There is no room to disgrace any person of Israel, as we have written above under the entry "Love of Fellows," and a person has no one to disgrace except himself, for it is fitting that he be despised in his own eyes, loathsome to himself, knowing and recognizing his own faults and blemishes. But the way of the world is the opposite - a person sees every affliction except his own affliction (Negaim 2:5), because a person is prone to search after his fellow's faults and immediately judges him unfavorably, but for himself he seeks forty-nine ways to purify the impure creeping thing, in a manner that it seems to him that his own deeds are pure and upright and there is none like him in all the land.
Pele Yoetz 25:2: And this is not the straight path - rather, it is fitting for an upright person to judge every person favorably, and to search thoroughly to find fault with himself. And if he does a small evil between himself and the Omnipresent or between himself and other people, let it grow great in his eyes, and let him not seek to minimize or diminish it, as the masters of ethics have written, that one should not look at the quantity of the transgression but at the greatness of the King who commanded regarding it, for for any transgression a person commits, he shall be called a rebel against the King of glory. And if he has studied much Torah and his hand has attained greatly, and he has excelled in performing mitzvot and good deeds, let all of it be small in his eyes compared to the greatness of his obligation according to his own understanding and ability, and compared to the smallness of his own worth and the smallness of his own care in doing things properly, with intention, fear, love, and great joy, as is required. Therefore let him always say with his mouth what matches his heart: I have done no good deed at all. And especially at the moment when those who are mistaken about him honor him, he must strengthen himself not to become proud, and at that moment he shall say in his heart: I know of myself that I am not worthy. And let him be despised in his own eyes, more loathsome than all creatures, even animals, for none of them provoke their Creator as he does - and all the more so let him be despised compared to young children, who have no sin - and even though he has mitzvot and good deeds to his credit, let him always worry that the loss may outweigh the gain. And our Sages, of blessed memory, already said (Ta'anit 20b) that one should not treat any person in the world with disgrace, for all are the handiwork of the Former of all, and everything the Holy One, blessed be He, created in His world, He created only for His own glory.
Pele Yoetz 25:3: And if others disgrace him, let him not be exacting at all and not go out to quarrel, but rather let him bow his head low and say: this is a sign to me that I am despised and loathsome before the Creator because of my sins, and He has sent this man to disgrace me, for the LORD told him to curse. And from another angle he shall gladden his heart, for the LORD desires to crush him with light afflictions, as though they involved no monetary loss, to finish off transgression and to complete atonement for sin, and great honor has been shown him from Heaven - provided he accept them with love and be joyful in such afflictions. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Gittin 36b) that of such men Scripture says (Judges 5:31), "and those who love Him are like the sun going forth in its might."
Pele Yoetz 25:4: And all the more so must one be careful and guard against being ungrateful and disgracing a person from whom he has received benefit, even the slightest benefit, under any circumstance. Go forth and learn from what they said (Berachot 50b) that one should not disgrace foods, and they said (Bava Kamma 92b): do not throw a stone into a well from which you have drunk. And Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, did not strike the river, because he had been saved by it, as it is written (Exodus 2:3), "and she placed it among the reeds by the bank of the river" - and likewise he did not strike the dust of the earth, because he had benefited from it in hiding the Egyptian in it. All the more so and how much more so regarding a person who did him good with definite intention, that his love for him should be preserved forever. And even if his fellow strikes him, he shall guard his own spirit and do everything that is incumbent upon him to do, and shall not say, "as he did to me, so shall I do to him, and I shall return his disgrace" - for this is a transgression in his hands, and nothing exempts him, and he loses much good. Therefore let him sit alone and be silent, for he who bears [insult in silence] receives great reward. And not only shall he be silent, but he shall not be exacting at all because of being disgraced, and his soul shall be like dust, until honor and disgrace are equal in his eyes. This is the attribute of equanimity - happy is he who attains this attribute, for there is no better attribute than this. And it was already told of one of the pious men, that they asked him on which day of his life he rejoiced with a joy greater than any other, and he answered that regarding bodily goods there is no room to rejoice, for all is utter vanity, and even what one thinks is good is bad and what one thinks is bad is good - and if there is reason to rejoice, it is over the good of the soul, and he had no greater good of the soul than this: one day he was sitting at the stern of a ship, and there were on the ship officers and wealthy men, and one of them wanted to urinate, and he went to the stern of the ship, and seeing him [the pious man] so despised in his eyes that he was not ashamed before him, he exposed himself and urinated on his face. And upon this pious man seeing that he had so acquired within his soul the attribute of equanimity that he was not exacting at all, then his heart rejoiced and his glory exulted over such a great good that he had acquired within his soul. And if one cannot restrain his spirit from being exacting, at least he can restrain his words. And this is what the commentators (Ibn Ezra) explained on the verse (Psalms 131:2), "surely I have stilled and quieted my soul" - that if I have not attained the attribute of equanimity, at least I have quieted myself, until his mind settles with pure thoughts to remove the exactingness from his heart entirely, and he shall attain gladness and joy.
Pele Yoetz 25:5: And all the more so must one be careful and guard against disgracing one to whom he is obligated in honor, such as his father and mother - for it is written (Deuteronomy 27:16), "cursed is he who dishonors his father and mother." And the halachic authorities wrote (Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 334, Bedek HaBayit) that although they said (Kiddushin 32a) that a father who forgoes his own honor, it is forgone - this refers specifically to his honor, but not to his disgrace. And alas for those wayward children who are found, who treat their father and mother with disgrace and cause them to gnash their teeth. Woe to such children on the day of judgment and the day of rebuke. And likewise one who disgraces his teachers. And one who disgraces a Torah scholar is liable to excommunication. And they said in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 100a): to what extent is disgracing a Torah scholar considered? For example, one who says "these rabbis" [disrespectfully]. And all the more so if he speaks against them erroneously. And how very much one must be careful, when writing about the words of our holy Rabbis, the earlier generations, whose littlest finger was thicker than our own loins, and when he does not understand their words, let him believe with complete faith that if there is an emptiness, it is in himself, that we do not fathom the depth of their understanding, and they are considered like our own Rabbis, from whose waters we drink and by whose mouths we live. Therefore let him be very careful, when writing about their words, to write with great honor, like a student arguing before his teacher on the ground [i.e., in utmost humility], and let him always regard himself as though the master of the tradition stood before him, and recognize his own place, and be ashamed and humbled and let trembling seize him, and be careful of their glowing coals lest he be burned.
Pele Yoetz 25:6: And go forth and learn how far the prohibition of the practice of disgrace extends - for it is written (Exodus 20:23), "and you shall not go up by steps to My altar, so that your nakedness not be exposed upon it." If the Torah was so exacting about the honor of the stones of the altar, which do not see and are not particular that a little of one's legs be exposed while ascending its steps, all the more so must one be careful in the presence of his father and mother, his teacher, a Torah scholar, and the like, not to sit before them in a disrespectful manner. And it is known that only under duress did they permit a son to recline in his father's presence on Passover night, while in his teacher's presence he is not permitted to recline even on Passover night (Pesachim 108a). And that well-known incident is known, where his teachers recognized him as a mamzer [child of a forbidden union] and a child of a menstruant woman, because he walked ahead of his teachers and treated them with a practice of disgrace and did not conduct himself with the honor befitting a student before his teacher, as brought in Avot D'Rabbi Natan - see there (Tractate Kallah Rabbati, ch. 2). Let the wise man hear and tremble and be seized [with fear], and be very careful with the honor of every person, and especially the honor of one to whom he is obligated in honor, and through this "the wise shall inherit honor" (Proverbs 3:35). (And more is written on this under the entries "Kavod" [honor] and "Mora" [reverence], for such is our way, to return to a subject.)
Pele Yoetz 26:1: Son - A son shall honor his father and mother, as we have written and shall write more of this - but now I come to summarize everything briefly, for there is no exposition without novelty. It is that there are commandments of the father toward the son to conduct himself with him according to his age, according to his character, according to the son's own understanding, and according to the need of the hour - whether requests or blessings - the father is obligated to conduct his affairs with judgment in a manner that this son shall do good and not sin. And for this, great understanding and extra patience are needed, to conduct himself according to need in a middle way, so that he neither refrains from disciplining a youth nor disciplines him too much, and neither cuts short where it is fitting to prolong nor prolongs where it is fitting to cut short. And it is likewise a commandment of the father toward the son to teach him Torah and to marry him off close to his coming of age (Kiddushin 29a), as we have written in its place.
Pele Yoetz 26:2: And it is the commandment of the son toward the father to honor him and fear him. And if sometimes his father becomes angry with him and strikes him and curses him for no reason, because of some distress in his heart from the incidents of the time, and his wrath is poured out upon him, or because of his father's own character or lack of understanding, then the son must have understanding to bear it all for the honor of his Maker's commandment, and shall not talk back to him nor answer him harshly nor humiliate him, God forbid, but shall bend his head like a reed and endure and not wither - for they said in the Talmud (Kiddushin 31a) of Dama ben Netina, that although he was a gentile and his mother was demented and slapped him in front of the great men of Rome and took his purse and threw it into the sea, he did not humiliate her. And how much more so if his father and mother are sensible people, the son must consider that they are justified in whatever they have done to him, and if it seems to him that they have gone out of line, this is due to his own lack of understanding - for such is the way of children, who always seek merit for themselves as though they were justified in everything they do, and it seems to them as though their father and mother are overriding justice against them in whatever they rebuke them for - but the son who has understanding and fear of the LORD, which is his own treasure, shall not think so nor consider so in his heart, but rather shall consider that they certainly, without doubt, act properly, and if there is any emptiness, it is his own. And he shall make his ear like a funnel to receive rebukes, and shall not deviate from what they tell him, right or left, even if it seems to him that they say of right that it is left.
Pele Yoetz 26:3: And it is likewise a commandment of the son to be a son who brings merit to his father (Sanhedrin 104a), and to strive with all his strength and all his might to send his father and mother to the Land of Israel and to honor them in their death, and whatever is in his power to do for their repose and the elevation of their souls, he shall do all the days of his life. These are some of the ways of righteousness by which sons and fathers should conduct themselves, for the honor of the King of glory.
Pele Yoetz 27:1: Daughter - I have seen an evil custom in these places, that when a daughter is born to a man, people increase in laughter and mockery. This one says, "what great cold [disappointment]," and that one says, "what great stench," and other such words of mockery - to the point that whoever has had a daughter born to him finds no place to hide from the extent of the pursuit with which they chase him with words of laughter and mockery. This deed is evil in my eyes; I apply to them [the verse] (Proverbs 17:5), "whoever mocks the poor blasphemes his Maker" - for these are the wonders of the One perfect in knowledge, who gives sons to whomever He wishes and daughters to whomever He wishes. It is found that whoever mocks the birth of daughters has spoken against the LORD Himself, besides the prohibition of mockery, which is great. And even greater than this is a great folly found among some ignorant people: if his wife bears a male, he loves her and honors her greatly, but if she bears a female, he distances her and does not come near her, and her abandonment and sorrow are great. How foolish are these men - what does he have against his wife? Did she go to the market and choose to buy him a daughter and not a son? And furthermore, why should he meddle with the "sheep of the Merciful One" [i.e. matters that are God's business] - is it not possible that daughters are actually preferable for her, since it may be that her fortune and her portion shall be good, as we have seen with our own eyes how many have rejoiced in a daughter among sons and her fortune was blessed more than the sons' - and "woe to him whose children are daughters" (Kiddushin 82b) is even worse today when there are many ignorant people and few who bear the yoke [of Torah], and many are the pains of the father of sons regarding Torah and the service of God - which is not so for the father of daughters, who has no such trouble with a daughter except to teach her women's work and good traits.
Pele Yoetz 27:2: And it is the father's commandment regarding his daughter to marry her off close to her coming of age, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 113a): if your daughter has come of age, free your slave and give her to him [in marriage] - and father and mother must stand guard over her with sevenfold vigilance so that her honor not be desecrated, for she desecrates her father [through improper conduct]. And it is a mitzvah to listen to the words of the Sages and hasten to marry them off as his means allow. And it is likewise the father's commandment to increase the dowry given to his daughter as his means allow, in order to find her a fitting match. And it is known, their saying, of blessed memory (Pesachim 49a): let a person always sell all that he has and marry his daughter to a Torah scholar.
Pele Yoetz 27:3: And there are many poor people whose souls desire to give their daughter to a Torah scholar, but what shall they do, since their hand cannot afford to give a dowry befitting the Torah scholar's need? Nevertheless, an obligation rests upon them to do everything in their power and to move mountains to gather enough to merit giving their daughter to a Torah scholar. And if they cannot do this, or if there is no Torah scholar to be found in their place, in any case let them choose a good young man, of worthy stock, literate and God-fearing, and let him not hand over his daughter to an ignorant person of evil deeds, for this is like throwing his daughter to the dogs, and her complaint against him shall be with her all the days of her life, for he has troubled her, "and one who troubles his own flesh is cruel" (Proverbs 11:17). And in the manner they said (Yevamot 63b[?]), "take a wife slowly" - so too one must be deliberate before giving his daughter to a man, and investigate him thoroughly until he knows for certain what kind of person he is, and see that he is good - then he shall give him his daughter. And it is true that "from the LORD is a wife for a man," and He mixes matches and settles the solitary in a home - nevertheless, this matter has already been explained below under the entry "Zivug" [match] - see there.
Pele Yoetz 27:4: And therefore an obligation rests upon every man to have mercy on his own soul and on the soul of his daughter, and to strive with all his strength to seek for her a resting place that shall be good for her and for him in this world and in the World to Come, and to pour out his soul before the LORD time and again for his sons and daughters, that the LORD match them with a fitting match (and I have already written a prayer for this, and appended it to my Beit Tefillati) - and also the daughter herself, if she knows how to write or read from a text, let her father go to a sage and arrange a prayer [for her] (and I shall also lift my hand to this, with the help of Heaven), or she herself, in private, shall weep for her own soul and afflict herself and pour out her soul before the LORD in words that come from her heart, whatever comes from her mouth, and pray to the LORD that He provide her a fitting match, a Torah scholar, and that she be given into the bosom of a God-fearing man, and that her match turn out well - and great is prayer for this matter. Go forth and learn from Leah, who was destined for Esau, but because she wept so much that Leah's eyes became tender, she fell to Jacob's lot (Bava Batra 123a), and she merited to establish six tribes from whom came the glory of Israel - the houses of priesthood and Levitical service and royal houses.
Pele Yoetz 27:5: And the daughter who is to be praised is one who does not set her eyes on wealth, but is content to be hungry and thirsty and naked and lacking everything, so long as her portion be with a Torah scholar who fears the LORD - therefore let her train herself accordingly, as befits the wife of a Torah scholar, that her eyes be generous, and that she not be exacting about pleasures of food nor about jewelry and the finery of garments, and let her accustom herself to sleeping little, speaking little, with carefulness, diligence, and other good traits, and the LORD too shall give her the good. And it is true that the Sages said (Ketubot 52b) that a person is obligated to adorn his daughter so that many shall pursue her - but the daughter who fears the LORD shall not show herself before young men, especially when she is adorned, so that they not stumble over her with sinful thoughts, and especially in these generations when the immodest have multiplied.
